newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans hit 8-1/2 year highs, coffee also soars. [CORRECTED 00:05 1/5]
newsitem.headline: Soybeans hit 8-1/2 year highs, coffee also soars. [CORRECTED 00:05 1/5]

text.p: Soybean prices soared to new 8-1/2 year highs on Wednesday and coffee jumped to 2-1/2 year highs as speculators and commercial firms stormed the market on worries about supplies.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for May delivery closed 22 cents a bushel higher at $8.89-1/2 after setting a new life-of-contract high at $8.93. That was the highest price for soybeans on the exchange since August 1988.

Prices soared from the opening after influential agricultural consultant Willard Sparks of Memphis, Tennessee-based Sparks Companies told an agricultural conference in Buenos Aires that he expected soybean prices to rise sharply.

Sparks said red-hot demand from domestic processors of soybeans and booming demand from overseas customers like China meant July futures in Chicago could rise as high as $9.75 a bushel. July futures ended at $8.87 Wednesday.

"I guess the world was startled back into the reality that we need to ration supply through higher prices," said Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter in Chicago. "Willard Sparks was telling the world that soybeans (are tight) and there were rumors about Chinese purchases again."

The Agriculture Department earlier this month said stocks of soybeans in the United States ahead of the new harvest next September 1 would fall to 125 million bushels, down from 140 million predicted a month earlier and 183 million last year.

Demand for soybean products -- soymeal for livestock feed and soyoils for food and myriad industrial uses -- has kept the "crush" rate at processors more than 10 percent above last year. Meanwhile, soybean exports are up 15 percent from 1996.

The soybean rally carried over to other grain markets. May delivery corn closed 3-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $2.95 and May oats rose 5-3/4 cents to $1.72-1/4, with both markets also supported by rain delays in planting forecasts for coming days.
Wheat for May delivery also soared, closing up 12 cents a bushel at $4.23.

A sale of 110,000 metric tons of U.S. wheat to an unknown overseas buyer was reported by exporters early in the day, bolstering sentiment that Pakistan could buy U.S. instead of Australian wheat when it tenders for 315,000 tons on Saturday.

Prices rose further late in the day when Oklahoma State University released a survey of wheat farmers estimating that 41 percent of the state's expected wheat crop was lost in the hard freeze that hit the Plains States on April 12-13.
Oklahoma production was now estimated at 121.3 million bushels this year, below the 205.4 million seen earlier.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee prices burst higher as supply worries sparked a wave of buying by speculators and commercial firms, traders said.

Coffee for May delivery closed 12.65 cents a pound higher at 239.05 cents, setting a life-of-contract high at 240 cents. That was the highest price for coffee since July 1994, when prices soared after a serious frost hit Brazil's crop.
"The market perceives there is no coffee around," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast. "And May's going through a squeeze because CSCE stocks are low and falling."

On Wednesday, the exchange reported that warehouse stocks of coffee certified for delivery against futures rose 565 bags to 47,668 bags as of April 29. But supplies remain down sharply from 83,000 bags three weeks ago.
May coffee contracts expire in three weeks, with the amount of coffee in stock far smaller than the existing number of futures contracts outstanding.
(Corrects to make clear coffee contracts expire in three weeks. Story originally claimed cash delivery period for May futures would begin in three weeks.)

"The rest of the market is following May," said South Futures president Stephen Smith. "A lot of people were short May going into notice period hoping the market was going to come off. There's only 2,000 (lots) open interest, but there's no coffee in certified stocks."
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed mostly lower with the exception of gasoline which rose after weekly stocks data showed a drawdown in supplies.
The American Petroleum Institute in a weekly report said U.S. gasoline stocks dropped almost 400,000 barrels in the week ended April 25, while crude oil stocks rose almost two million barrels.

Unleaded gasoline for May delivery closed 0.55 cent a gallon higher at 63.91 cents while crude oil for June delivery fell 23 cents a barrel to close at $20.21. May heating oil closed 0.84 cent a gallon lower at 58.07 cents.
